title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (6 of 7)
hook: the wind can't move a blade of grass, and when Indra comes near, the stranger vanishes
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaksha: the gods took the credit, a wondrous being appeared, and Agni, who could burn the earth, couldn't burn one blade of grass.

Fire came back empty-handed, and the gods are sure the next one will crack it. He's stronger. He has more reach. And when he fails too, they send their king. What happens to the king is the strangest turn in the whole story, because he doesn't fail the way the others did.
screen: `THE NEXT ONE WILL CRACK IT.` → `THEN THE WIND.` → `THEN THE KING.`

segments.voice: The gods turn to Vayu, the wind. Vayu, find out what this wondrous being is. He runs up. Who are you? I am Vayu, the one who moves through the sky. What power is in you? I could carry off everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The same blade of grass is set down. Carry this off. Vayu rushes at it with all his speed, and can't move it. He comes back: I couldn't find out. Then the gods turn to Indra, king of the gods. Maghavan, find out what this being is. Indra runs toward it, and the being vanishes. No question, no blade of grass, no test. Just gone. Why vanish for Indra? The text doesn't say, and commentators offer reasons. One common reading: Indra was the proudest of all, the king, so he's made to wait, and learn humility. Another: he was already closer, and the next teaching needs a different teacher. Either way, the king is left standing in empty space. And there, in that same space, he meets a woman. The text calls her very radiant, or richly adorned, and names her: Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya. It's one of the earliest times in Hindu scripture that Uma appears by name, and many later Hindus hear in her the goddess Parvati, Shiva's consort, the divine mother. Indra asks her the question none of the gods could answer: what was that wondrous being? Her answer comes tomorrow. Fire and wind tried to measure the mystery by their own power. Indra came nearer, lost the mystery, and was given a teacher.
screen: `THE WIND CAN'T MOVE IT.` · `THE KING COMES, AND IT VANISHES.` · `A WOMAN IN THE EMPTY SPACE.` · `UMA, DAUGHTER OF THE HIMALAYA.` · then, large: `WHAT WAS THAT BEING?`

segments.voice: Think of a time something you were chasing slipped away, an answer, a plan, a feeling of certainty, and stay with the empty space it left without rushing to fill it. In the story, the empty space is exactly where the teacher appears. If a thought rushes in to fix things, let it pass, and come back to the open space.
Uma Haimavati, Uma, daughter of Himavat. The wind cannot move the grass; the king comes near and the being vanishes; and there, Indra meets Uma, radiant, daughter of the Himalaya.
Your line: the one behind the ear. An empty space can be the start of an answer. That's day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially in Shaiva and Shakta traditions, honor Uma Haimavati in the Kena as an early appearance of the goddess, the divine mother who teaches the gods.
